lesson.title: Bracket Sentences in the Wild
lesson.subtitle: Ich kann morgen kommen — one frame, three facts, zero effort

hook.title: The Sentence Sandwich
hook.content: German grammar hands you a machine: the conjugated modal opens the sentence, the bare infinitive closes it, and everything you want to say lives in between. Ich kann morgen kommen says WHO (ich), WHAT (kommen), WHEN (morgen) and CAN — four facts in one breath. English needs three verbs for that. German needs one. The closing infinitive is called the Satzklammer — the sentence bracket — because it clamps around your message like a staple.

footnotes.title: A Frame You Will Meet Again
footnotes.content: The same bracket architecture returns when Germans talk about the past (Ich habe... gegessen) — the tense verb opens, the participle closes. Master it now with modals and the past tense will feel like a rerun.

pattern.title: Build the Bracket
pattern.content:
Slot 1 is the subject, slot 2 the conjugated modal, then the contents, then the bare infinitive slams shut at the end: Ich kann morgen wandern. Wir wollen heute singen. Ich muss lernen. Du kannst folgen. Nothing else in the sentence may leave the bracket — time words like morgen (twin of 'morrow', the word inside to-morrow) and heute (today) ride inside it, usually right after the verb. The frame never breaks: no matter how full the middle gets, the infinitive waits at the caboose.

One Denglisch ladder, read it the German way first: Ich kann morgen kommen → I can tomorrow come → I can come tomorrow. The odd middle line is exact German — modal in position 2, contents inside, bare infinitive at the caboose — and Old English allowed every word of it.
pattern.linguist_note: English did this too — archaic 'I can go' survives, but Middle English also allowed 'I can the road go' patterns; modern English lost the bracket by fusing modals with a to-infinitive. German kept the original Germanic frame intact.

exercises.prompt: In 'Ich will Deutsch lernen', why does 'lernen' sit at the very end?
options: Old words go last in German
The bare infinitive always closes the modal bracket
Deutsch pushed it out of position 2
exercises.target_answer: The bare infinitive always closes the modal bracket
exercises.meaning: The Satzklammer: modal in position 2, bare infinitive last
exercises.explanation: The conjugated modal opens the frame; the bare infinitive clamps it shut. Everything else lives inside.

exercises.prompt: Match each bracket sentence with its English meaning:
exercises.target_answer: Ich kann morgen wandern, Wir wollen heute singen, Ich muss lernen, Du kannst folgen, Du musst aussteigen, Wir wollen fernsehen, ich habe Lust auf Wurst, Ich will ein Bier
exercises.meaning: I can hike tomorrow, we want to sing today, I have to learn, you can follow, you must get off, we want to watch TV, I feel like sausage, I want a beer
exercises.explanation: Modal in position 2, contents inside, bare infinitive at the end — the same frame every time, even for new verbs like aussteigen and fernsehen.

exercises.prompt: Close the bracket: 'Wir können morgen _____' (to board / get on):
exercises.english_hint: the bare infinitive rides at the end
exercises.meaning: Wir können morgen einsteigen = We can board tomorrow
exercises.explanation: The bare infinitive 'einsteigen' closes the bracket — ein + steigen, 'climb on', kept as one word. No zu, no ending.

exercises.prompt: The German time word 'morgen' hides inside an English adverb — which word is its twin?
exercises.meaning: morrow — as in to-morrow (twin of German morgen)
exercises.explanation: English 'tomorrow' is literally 'to the morrow'; German morgen never needed the 'to'.

exercises.idea: you're eyeing the cake at the bakery and guessing about the price: it can be expensive
cues: The thing → der Kuchen (der is the masculine flag)
The bare infinitive closes the bracket: sein goes last
exercises.explanation: kann holds position 2, the bare infinitive sein closes the bracket — and teuer is 'dear' with its d hardened to t.

summary.outcome: Build full modal brackets with time words: who, what, when, and can/want/must in one frame.

use_example.english: I want to learn German tomorrow.

summary.takeaway: Conjugated modal in position 2, bare infinitive last — the bracket carries your whole message.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the first great sound shift — how English 'hope' breathed into 'hoffen' and 'ship' into 'Schiff'.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Bracket Sentences in the Wild (The cake can be expensive):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Der Kuchen kann teuer sein" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Bracket Sentences in the Wild without relying on short-term echo.

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

können.context_translation: I can come / I am able to come.
können.etymology_derivation: Originally meant "to know/understand". Preserved in English "can", "cunning" (knowing how), "uncanny", and "beyond my ken" (beyond my knowledge).

wollen.etymology_derivation: Retains original Germanic sense of desire/intent: "free will", "will to live", "against my will", and "willingly" (cf. Latin voluntary).

müssen.context_translation: I must / have to go now.
müssen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English "must" (root shifted to sibilant -ss-).

wandern.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *wandarōn — German kept the full -ern ending that English wore down to -er. [wiktionary]

lernen.context_translation: I am learning German with Brücke.
lernen.etymology_derivation: Shared root *liznōną (to follow a track/learn) + infinitive -en.

folgen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fulgāną — English softened the ancient g into w (follow), German kept it spelled out. Takes the dative. [wiktionary]

fernsehen.etymology_derivation: fern + sehen — literally far-seeing; the entry calls it a calque of French télévision, the same idea as English television. [wiktionary]

einsteigen.context_phrase: Wir steigen in den Bus ein.
einsteigen.etymology_derivation: ein (in) + steigen (to climb): to climb in — German pictures boarding as climbing aboard; the climb-verb is native German. [wiktionary]

aussteigen.context_phrase: Ich steige an der nächsten Station aus.
aussteigen.context_translation: I get off at the next stop.
aussteigen.etymology_derivation: aus (out) + steigen (to climb): to climb out and off the train, bus or tram. [wiktionary]

deutsch.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz, of the people, built on *þeudō, people; the very same word as English Dutch, with Latin theodiscus and Teutonic sharing the root. [wiktionary]

bier.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *beuzą. Medial ie produces pure tense monophthong [iː].

kuchen.context_translation: Would you like a piece of cake?
kuchen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *kōkô; Wiktionary names only Dutch koek — see Apfelkuchen. [wiktionary]

wurst.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *wursti; English wurst is only a later borrowing from German — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

lust.context_translation: I feel like having ice cream.
lust.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *lustuz — the explicit twin of English lust; in German it just means desire (Lust haben). [wiktionary]

teuer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *diurijaz — the true twin of English dear (d → t). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
